extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Use Orson Scott Card's MICE Quotient framework to identify a story's dominant type (Milieu, Idea, Character, or Event), shape beginning and ending points, manage nested threads and try/fail cycles, and choose/adhere to a POV contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant story type (MICE Quotient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story is dominated by one of four story-types (M — Milieu, I — Idea, C — Character, E — Event). The type determines the structure: where it begins, where it ends, what counts as resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose which letter dominates your story and let that determine the narrative arc. If the dominant type is unclear or shifts unpredictably, the story will feel unfocused. Examples: Milieu stories emphasize place/world; Idea stories revolve around a question; Character stories revolve around transformation; Event stories revolve around disruption and restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milieu (M) — setting-driven structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is fundamentally about a place/world/setting. Begins when the protagonist enters the milieu; ends when they leave it. Resolution is exit or return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use world-revealing scenes as your narrative beats; emphasize how the setting changes or affects the character. Example works: Gulliver's Travels; Le Guin's The Dispossessed. Anti-pattern: treating setting as background ornament rather than the central problem/opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea (I) — question-driven structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is fundamentally about a question — a mystery, discovery, or puzzle. Begins when the question is posed; ends when it is answered. Resolution = answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the central question explicit (or felt) early and build try/fail cycles around attempts to answer it. Detective stories and 'what is the secret?' plots fit here. Anti-pattern: introducing multiple central questions that dilute resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (C) — transformation-driven structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is fundamentally about a transformation of identity, role, or relationship. Begins when the character grows dissatisfied with their current self; ends when they have a new self or accept the old one. Resolution = self-knowledge/change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus scenes on inner conflict and choices that reveal growth or failure to change. Ensure the protagonist's arc is clearly tied to narrative events. Anti-pattern: external events happen but do not cause meaningful internal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event (E) — disruption-driven structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is fundamentally about something disrupting the world's order. Begins with the disruption (or its first symptom); ends when order is restored or replaced. Resolution = new equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the disruption and its consequences as the engine of plot; show the process of restoration or replacement of order. Anti-pattern: resolving disruption without addressing its broader consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure alignment with type (beginning/ending/resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's opening and closing must align with its dominant MICE type — where the story begins, where it ends, and what counts as resolution are determined by the type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or revising, check that the inciting moment corresponds to the type's defined beginning and that the ending delivers the type's resolution (exit/answer/change/new equilibrium). Misaligned openings/closings create a felt mismatch between promise and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nesting threads (LIFO closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sub-threads can be nested as MICE codes within a larger MICE thread. Each opened thread must be closed in last-in-first-out (LIFO) order, like brackets. Unclosed threads = unsatisfying ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track sub-threads and ensure you resolve the most recently opened sub-thread before resolving earlier ones. Use the bracket model (e.g., M{ I{ C{ ...resolve C...} ...resolve I...} ...resolve M...}) to map openings and closings. Anti-pattern: leaving inner threads unresolved while closing outer arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try/fail cycles within threads
rubrics_metrics.description: Within each MICE thread, the protagonist tries to resolve the question/problem and fails (or partially succeeds with a new complication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include about 2–3 try/fail cycles per thread to tighten plot tension and show progression. Each failure should raise stakes or reveal new information, not merely repeat the same attempt. Anti-pattern: a single attempt that resolves everything or many attempts with no escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view selection and contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a POV form (first person, third-person limited, third-person omniscient, cinematic/external, or multiple viewpoint). Each carries a different contract with the reader about what can and cannot be revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the POV that best serves your dominant MICE type and keep the POV's 'contract' consistent — e.g., don't reveal internal thoughts in cinematic scenes or switch omniscient knowledge without signposting. Multiple viewpoints are acceptable but must be handled deliberately (clear alternation, purpose). Audit whether the POV honors its contract; violations frustrate reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Key elements for building strong characters: what the character wants, what they need (often different from what they want), what they fear, what stands in their way, and what they will pay to achieve their goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make these elements explicit in scenes and decisions so motivations and stakes feel real. Use them to drive try/fail cycles and to justify transformation in a C-story. Anti-patterns: flat goals, unstated needs, or unclear costs that make choices feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story diagnostic checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact evaluation method: identify the dominant MICE letter; check whether opening and closing align with that type; verify nesting order is preserved; count try/fail cycles; audit whether POV honors its contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when diagnosing drafts. For each item, mark pass/fail and note revisions: e.g., change opening to match type, close unclosed threads, add or escalate try/fail cycles, or fix POV leaks. This combines the above metrics into a single practical audit.
